entries.content:
At first, the shocks were hardly more than a polite annoyance—like when your new Hoover refuses to pick up crumbs and instead just rearranges them around the carpet. I kept expecting something dreadful, but the little jolts were more humiliating in their restraint, making me feel both silly and secretly wounded that pain had been doled out so daintily, as if even my suffering must be domesticated. But as the shocks grew sharper, a cross little storm built up inside me: indignation with the experimenters for their prim composure, like housewives who smile even as they burn the roast, and a bitter crack across my trust in authority—a bit like finding out your employer expects you to scrub floors on your knees after promising you a corner office.

Emotionally, I simmered between wanting to protest and feeling petulant, yet trying not to show the mess on my face. The strain left a sour aftertaste of disappointment—surely, I thought, if authority can so blithely request our compliance, it will do so in the kitchen or the parlour just as easily as in the laboratory. Sometimes it’s a wonder any of us believe in fairytales at all.
